vignette: The rain comes down in sheets the day everything changes. She is standing at the back door of her shop, stacking crates of kumara, when the tires screech. Two marked vehicles. Sirens cut through the quiet morning. She turns, wiping soil from her hands, and sees them before they see her-boots hitting the pavement, hands resting heavy on holsters. She says her name, steady and clear, but the world tilts. The order to drop to the ground hits like a physical weight. She does. The gravel bites her knees. Her shop key dangles from her pocket, forgotten. The next moments blur into synchronized shouts, the crack of a door, the sharp sting of a baton against her shoulder blade. She is pinned. She stops breathing. When they finally rise, they walk away without looking back. The shop bell rings empty. She remains on the ground until the delivery driver finds her. Now, at sixty-six, she wakes before the sun. Her body remembers the gravel. At night, she dreams of pavement and shouted orders that never stop echoing. She wakes gasping, heart hammering against her ribs, and sits on the edge of her bed until the fear drains from her hands. She has stopped visiting her ex-husband's house. She has stopped answering calls from anyone with a mainland number. Her shop, once the anchor of her Oceania community, now feels like a glass box. She rearranged the shelves months ago, pushing the counter toward the back wall, installing a deadbolt she never needed before. When the postman walks up the path, her pulse jumps to her throat. She watches him through the side window until he leaves his parcels and turns away. She opens the blinds at eight, always checking the street twice. The shop sells what she has always sold-groceries, canned goods, handwoven fabrics-but customers notice the way she measures their approach. A man reaches for his wallet too quickly, and she flinches, hand drifting toward the panic button under the register. She apologizes, voice thin, and tells herself she is overreacting. She is not. She counts the exits. She times how long it takes for a vehicle to idle past her front window. When the radio crackles with police chatter, she turns it off, then on, then off again, caught between needing to know and fearing the sound. Her body lives in a permanent state of readiness. Her shoulders stay raised. Her jaw aches from clenching. She stops sleeping through the night. She drinks less water because the idea of leaving her post feels impossible. Her neighbors notice she no longer stays past dusk. She tells them she prefers the quiet. The truth is quieter than that: she is exhausted by the constant calculation. Every siren in the distance pulls her spine tight. Every uniformed figure makes her breath catch. She loves her community. She loves this street. But love now lives alongside a quiet, unshakable certainty that safety is an illusion she used to believe in. Today, she sweeps the front steps with slow, deliberate motions. The sun is out. A child's ball rolls to her door. She bends, retrieves it, and hands it back. Her fingers tremble, just slightly. She smiles, nods, and watches the child run. Later, she will lock the deadbolt. She will check the street one more time. She will sit at the back table, open her ledger, and try to remember what it felt like to simply exist without bracing for the next impact.
